style: trading psychology coach (Conscious Trading Academy)
markets: general / not market specific
edge_principles: Judge a strategy only on periods where its rules were actually followed; rule-breaking makes the sample meaningless.
Reframe a rules-based stop-out as a correct (winning) execution, which lowers the emotional cost of exiting on time.
Every loss should yield a written lesson and a concrete adjustment, captured in a journal along with the emotion felt.
Watch for P&L 'ceilings' where a trader repeatedly self-sabotages near a familiar profit level; same setup, different behavior.
Pre-market mental rehearsal of how to act at the exit point, in a calm state, to make rule adherence automatic.
notes: Coaching conversation with co-host Tessa about failing to exit a losing position; entirely about mindset, conditioning and emotional regulation. No trading setups.

style: ex-prop (Chopper/DRW, SMB intern), independent volatility trader
markets: crypto options and futures (Deribit), VIX products, treasury basis, grain options
edge_principles: Trade for income, not compounding: keep a fixed low-six-figure account and withdraw profits each year so one blow-up cannot erase a decade.
Volatility mean-reverts, so the question becomes timing not direction; the 'obvious' trade is often expensive to carry (contango), so lean counter-intuitive.
Fade reactive moves in one-off events where quant models have no history; leg into mean-reversion positions over days rather than one clip.
When selling options, buy a cheap short-dated far-OTM 'throwaway' hedge against the extra short unit.
After a bad drawdown: flatten, stop trading for weeks and take a mental break rather than sizing up to win it back.
Edges are noisy and decay as new participants arrive; exploit structural mispricings while they last.
notes: Options/vol specialist: crypto skew collars, cash-and-carry basis, perp-discount convergence, put 1x2 after vol spikes, selling overpriced event vol. Nothing intraday for US stocks.

style: contrarian macro / futures trader (Crowded Market Report), ex-hedge fund
markets: futures: currencies, bonds, stock indices, commodities
edge_principles: Fixed risk per trade (0.7% of equity) on every signal regardless of conviction; he finds no reliable way to rank which trades will work and his most-hated trades often work best.
Low win rate (37-40%) is fine when winners are several times losers; one 7R winner pays for seven losers.
Only trade when the edge condition exists (extreme positioning); when it goes neutral, exit and sit out instead of trading out of boredom.
Wait for the market to confirm the thesis (reaction to news) rather than fighting the tape.
Re-entry after a stop is allowed only on a fresh signal, never by averaging.
Knowing less macro story can help: follow the process, not your narrative.
notes: Core setup is a counter-trend 'news failure' reversal day in a market where COT positioning is at an extreme; daily futures, multi-week holds.

style: head trader, Maverick Trading (prop); trend follower
markets: US stocks, ETFs, options, forex
edge_principles: Exits/position management matter more than entries: a year-long live test with random tickers and a mechanical ATR trailing stop was still profitable.
Expect streaks: with a ~40% win rate, 10-11 losses in a row happen; the biggest winner came right after the longest losing streak, so skipping signals after losses is costly.
Use defined-risk structures (options) or automated stops when you know you break rules 1 time in 10.
Design rules around known personal flaws (overtrading after win streaks, sizing up) rather than relying on willpower.
Match indicator speed to stop width (e.g. 13 EMA with a 2xATR stop).
Too much research creates attachment that makes exiting harder.
notes: Flat Earth Trading Society experiment: 100 randomly picked tickers, direction by 13-EMA slope, 1% risk, 2xATR trailing stop with tightening; +15%, 40% win rate, PF 1.38. Also a multi-timeframe trend + relative strength stock selection rule.

style: independent intraday index futures trader (confluence / options-exposure levels)
markets: NQ, ES futures and CFDs; SPY/QQQ options data
edge_principles: Only one good impulse move per day is needed; cap at 1-2 trades and stop once you have it.
Size by volatility: same dollar risk (~1%/day) every day, so contracts shrink on high-vol days (Fed speakers, CPI).
Require both the stop and the target to make sense (min ~2-3R) or skip the trade.
Avoid the middle 50% between key levels where price chops; act only at levels.
Take half off at the next level and trail the rest; accept 1.5-2R if the trail is hit.
Curve-fitted intraday indicator scripts degraded in forward tests; he dropped them.
Cut quickly when price moves rapidly against you; journal how long losers vs winners were held.
notes: Pre-market checklist (open location vs options-exposure levels, R:R, confluence of VIX/DXY/Mag-7) to catch one NY-session impulse in NQ/ES.

style: discretionary global macro (ex-ING $20bn fixed income, Palinuro Capital)
markets: bonds, FX, rates, equity indices, commodities
edge_principles: Being right is not sufficient; the edge is surprising consensus pricing, so measure how crowded a view is before trading it.
Plan exits for winners and for time: on negative-carry trades set a time stop for how long you will pay carry, not only a price stop.
Risk = probability x magnitude: 'near-certain' arbitrages still need small size because the rare break is large.
Correlations go to one in deleveraging events; stress-test the portfolio for that, not for average historical correlation.
Screen many markets with systems; manual monitoring is error-prone.
Single-variable narratives (e.g. global liquidity) have ~zero statistical power for forward equity returns.
notes: Macro framework talk; two semi-systematic signals: carry-basket Sharpe ratio as a crowding/drawdown warning, and screening correlated pairs for broken reactions after big news.

style: swing/growth trader (Minervini school), RTM Capital
markets: US stocks, long side
edge_principles: Start with real money at small size, prove an edge over a sample, then let the evidence justify larger size; paper trading omits the emotional half.
Judge plans over many trades, not today's outcome; a simple plan you follow beats an intricate one you abandon.
Keep stops tight (max 8-10%, long-run average under 5%) and do not sell a well-acting winner for less than your average gain.
Give the benefit of the doubt to positions that put you under no pressure; cut the laggards, not the leaders.
Leadership stocks breaking down give early warning to raise cash before broad bear markets.
Re-entry after a stop is fine but wait a day or two for volatility to settle and a new base to form.
notes: Minervini-style long-only swing trading: manual screens of 600-1000 names, Stage-2 uptrends, tight consolidation pivots, small stops.

style: retail quant, small-cap intraday short seller
markets: US small caps
edge_principles: Start from repeated screen-time observations, then quantify them by hand-collecting data (he used thinkorswim OnDemand) before trusting them.
Run the model ~90% mechanically; the only discretion is disqualifying odd gappers (buyouts, flat-lined news gaps).
Reset risk daily to current account size; size up when the edge is proven but respect liquidity: slippage at 100k+ share sizes marks the capacity ceiling.
A large daily loss that is inside the model's expected distribution is not a reason to change the model.
Sector/sympathy risk: several correlated small caps squeezing together can hit a short book at once.
Edges erode and regimes change (2022-23 flat after 2020 boom); keep researching new models.
notes: Grew $10k to $3.8M (2019-2021) shorting intraday hyper-extensions in overnight small-cap gappers with a precise time-of-day entry; did not reveal exact rules.

style: fully automated systematic trader (55 systems), author
markets: US stocks, ETFs, commodity futures
edge_principles: Run many uncorrelated systems (trend/mean-reversion, long/short, short/long lookbacks) instead of tweaking one; more trade frequency also shortens drawdowns.
Do not re-optimise after a bad six months; recency-biased tweaks lag the regime.
Allocate equally across systems to avoid recency bias toward the best backtest.
Expect live drawdown to be at least double the simulated maximum; size for that.
Distrust mean-reversion backtests that show no big losers or whose profits come from fat tails - something was filtered.
Keep 'insurance' systems that lose a little most years but pay in sharp sell-offs.
Systems you build yourself are the ones you can keep trading through drawdowns.
notes: Systematic portfolio-of-systems philosophy; gives the architecture (trend long, MR long, MR short, trend short hedge, commodity trend, crash system) but few exact parameters.

style: independent event-driven / merger-arb news trader (ex-First New York)
markets: US stocks in announced or rumored M&A; side project in futures positioning
edge_principles: Trade only where you are already up to speed; an unfamiliar headline is a reason to add the name to the watch list, not to trade it.
News edge decays within seconds to minutes once it is widely distributed - treat it like an hourglass and do nothing after it runs out.
Keep a detailed log of every news trade: category, size, time of day, fast vs idea trade.
Analyst price targets for takeovers had no statistical value in his own tally.
Quiet periods are his 'drawdowns'; resist trading index ETFs out of boredom.
Have a hard daily dollar loss line; giving 'a bit more room' tends to triple the loss.
notes: Event-driven scalper: tracks 75-100 announced deals and rumoured situations; buys confirmed deals before the large arb funds finish their analysis, fades over-reactions to already-known or toothless news.

style: CANSLIM growth trader, ex-William O'Neil PM, TraderLion co-founder
markets: US growth stocks; Nasdaq/S&P for market timing
edge_principles: Market direction is about half the game; three of four stocks follow the market, so gate long exposure on a market-timing signal.
Max loss 7-8% from buy point; failed breakouts of real leaders rarely go below that even when they need several attempts.
Fit rules to each stock's 'personality' (which moving average it respects); avoid stocks you repeatedly lose on even if they are great.
Use sentiment extremes only when at least three indicators agree; otherwise defer to the action of the leaders.
Count of quality setups and leaders' stage tells you whether a follow-through day is real.
Pyramiding by adding every +2.5% on breakouts now tends to get shaken out; adapt to higher volatility.
notes: CANSLIM refresher with concrete follow-through-day rule, relative-strength-line-leads-price signal, and a moving-average two-day-undercut exit rule.

style: ex-prop floor trader (Gibraltar), now 'pro retail' CFD/FX scalper
markets: indices, FX, commodities via retail CFD platforms (8 products)
edge_principles: Classify every trade by time budget: scalp (<=15 min), average (<=2 h), day trade (<=8 h); size inversely to time in market.
Prop desks use a daily money stop (e.g. lose X in the morning, sit out until afternoon) rather than % per trade.
Set a monthly money target and work it back to daily and per-trade size so effort is worth the screen time.
Do not trade the data number itself; wait for the market reaction, then trade the pullback or continuation.
Avoid boredom trades: be at the screen only when alerts or scheduled volatility justify it.
Biggest losses came from ego-holding a data trade that 'had to' turn.
notes: Mostly about size, speed and psychology. One loosely specified fade setup: short spikes into predefined Fibonacci-extension extremes, scaling in, taking first profit offered. ~80% of trades are shorts.

style: trading psychologist / hedge fund coach; active short-term index trader
markets: S&P 500 (ES) intraday/short-term; coaches multi-strat hedge funds
edge_principles: Daily review: one thing done well to repeat, one thing to improve, with a concrete plan.
Place stops where the trade idea is objectively invalidated, not at a fixed percentage.
When volatility, volume or cross-market correlations shift meaningfully, treat it as a new regime and step back from risk.
Re-size for volatility; practise high-volatility regimes via bar-by-bar replay before risking money.
After a well-researched idea loses, assume you missed something and find it before trading again.
Breadth divergence (index highs with fewer sectors/stocks participating) has preceded major tops (2000, 2007).
Capital allocators value Sharpe, smoothness and uniqueness of returns, not raw P&L.
Match style to cognitive strengths (fast pattern recognisers scalp; slow analysts invest).
notes: Mostly psychology and process; gives one short-term index pattern (multi-timeframe overbought failure / right-shoulder entry) and a breadth-based regime read.

style: options income trader / educator; buy-and-hold investor
markets: ES futures options, large-cap US stock options, ETFs
edge_principles: Split capital into fast/medium/slow buckets (index credit spreads, cash-secured puts on blue chips, buy-and-hold), roughly a third each, so some bucket works in every regime.
Capital preservation first; never use broker leverage; cap max spread loss at <= 50% of capital.
Reduce exposure ahead of known unpredictable events (policy announcements) instead of trusting option deltas.
When volatility jumps, keep the same premium target but move strikes further away, or shorten expiries in fast markets.
Restrict universe to very large caps (>= $20-50B) to avoid blow-ups.
notes: Options income approach: far OTM ES credit spreads (~10% away) on 1-2 month cycles plus wheel-style puts on mega caps. No intraday stock setups.

style: systematic FX mean-reversion trader (ex-institutional), World Cup FX runner-up
markets: G10 FX crosses (CAD/NOK, AUD/NOK, AUD/CAD)
edge_principles: Only run mean-reversion on assets with a structural reason to mean-revert (economically linked currencies); oscillators on trending assets (e.g. equity indices) are overfit.
Fixed position size without compounding: absolute max drawdown stays constant so its percentage shrinks as profits accumulate.
Scale into mean-reversion entries in thirds as deviation grows; lowers profit when the first entry is right but survives bigger excursions.
Use a systematic wide stop to survive black swans; keep trading through them if sized for historical worst case.
Pair a mean-reversion book with a trend-following book on structurally trending assets to cut portfolio drawdown.
Competition results are inflated by ~2x leverage and house-money sizing; do not copy into real accounts.
notes: One concrete strategy: mean-reversion on commodity-linked FX crosses with take-profit at the moving average, about 10 trades per year, trading since ~2012.

style: CTA / commodity futures trend trader since late 1980s
markets: commodity futures (softs, grains, metals, energy), some stocks
edge_principles: Prefer quiet, less-covered markets (softs) over headline markets to avoid news-driven whipsaws.
Keep losses small and avoid drawdowns >10%; tell clients you are standing aside when conditions do not suit your style.
Think in percentages, not dollars, so big unrealised P&L does not trigger premature exits.
If clearly bullish news fails to lift price, tighten the stop or expect to be stopped (and vice versa).
Rising price with rising volume and rising open interest = new longs entering; trade with them.
Indicators mostly serve as emotional comfort; price itself carries the information.
Think in expected value (40% accuracy with 3:1 or 30% with 5:1 is fine); re-assess odds conditionally as a trade progresses.
Measure P&L against an hourly wage to keep perspective on whether scalping profits justify the time.
notes: Self-taught commodity trend trader; one concrete mechanism: risk-neutral pyramiding (add units while trailing stops so total open risk never exceeds the initial risk).

style: retired pro intraday futures scalper (news/price action), MenthorQ mentor
markets: NQ, ES futures
edge_principles: When VIX is extreme (5-min ES ATR ~10x normal), cut size drastically, move to micros/ETFs or stand aside until volatility comes down.
In high volatility, normal stops get hit in a minute; repeated re-entries escalate into revenge sizing and blow-ups.
On news-driven days a fixed take-profit can cut off the big news candle; he prefers a hard stop with no fixed target (and is annoyed when he breaks that rule).
If you keep losing in a particular session window (e.g. straight after work), change the time you trade.
Daily review: one biggest lesson, how to be 1% better tomorrow, extreme ownership of each rule break.
Judge educators by a multi-year verified record trading their own money; prop-evaluation payouts net of failed challenges can hide losses.
notes: Community/mentoring and psychology episode; no concrete entry setup given. Main operational takeaways are volatility-scaled sizing and avoiding fixed targets on news days.

style: options trader (Outlier Trading), Marine veteran
markets: US equity and index options (SPX 0DTE, single-stock earnings), futures
edge_principles: Trade 'profit mechanisms' (observable, explainable market effects), then quantify their normal behavior (mean/median/min/max day-over-day) so exits are data-driven.
Exit when the mechanism is not behaving as normal (e.g. IV not rising on schedule) - do not morph a losing options trade into a new structure.
Treat outcomes driven by unrelated shocks as 'no information' for the strategy being tested.
Spread small size across many independent trades per cycle to reduce path dependency.
Size short-premium trades so the worst historical move (and a bit worse) costs < 1% of the portfolio; add a cheap wing on the side with fat-tail risk.
Paper-track alternative structures alongside live trades to build a data set.
Use after-hours futures to hedge single-name event risk (e.g. short NQ against a bad NVDA print).
notes: Three ways to trade one earnings release: pre-earnings IV run-up, post-release IV crush, and post-earnings announcement drift.

style: intraday futures/FX quant + order-flow prop trader (Apex Capital)
markets: CME futures (NQ, ES, NG, GC, CL), FX
edge_principles: Robustness pipeline: in-sample build, separate out-of-sample tests, walk-forward optimisation, then non-consecutive sample testing on a much larger set; think in data points (5-10k), not years.
Every variable needs a logical reason; knowing why a strategy works tells you when it should not (e.g. breakouts need volume).
Risk per trade = target max drawdown / (Monte-Carlo worst losing streak x 1.2-1.3 realism factor).
Scale size up when the strategy's driving variable is strong (high relative volume) and cut to 1/2-1/3 when it is weak (summer, holidays).
Edge first, then risk management turns good into great; risk management cannot fix a strategy without edge.
Bought/off-the-shelf strategies rarely carry real edge; building your own teaches how to fix it when it breaks.
notes: Order-flow and systematic intraday futures; concrete ideas: gate opening-range breakouts on cumulative volume vs 100-day average, and absorption fades when heavy aggressive buying fails to close above a level.

style: position trader / newsletter (The Technical Traders), former futures day trader
markets: index ETFs (SPY, QQQ), bonds (TLT), US dollar, cash
edge_principles: Trade only a few (5-12) end-of-day signals a year on liquid index ETFs; signals computed after close, executed next open.
Scale allocation inversely to volatility (e.g. 30% higher vol -> ~30% smaller allocation; in 2008 half size with double stop and target).
When volatility rises, move down an asset hierarchy to slower assets (stocks > bonds > dollar > cash).
Follow price over opinion: can be bearish but long if the trend is up.
Utilities and staples outperforming for days to weeks often precede an equity leg down; gold outperforming equities warns of a larger reset.
Bear-market shorts should be brief (5-10 days) because counter-rallies are violent.
Take partial profits at Fibonacci targets and trail the rest.
notes: Asset-rotation position strategy using trend, cross-asset sentiment (11 assets/ratios) and position management. One testable framework: rotate among SPY/QQQ, TLT, UUP, cash with volatility-scaled allocation.

style: ICT-method discretionary FX and index futures trader; record prop-firm payouts
markets: FX (EUR/USD, GBP), index futures (NQ, ES)
edge_principles: Few trades (1-3 per week) with a weekly plan built from the economic calendar; one idea, one entry - repeated re-entries on the same idea bleed out.
Know when not to trade: sit out when intermarket signals (yields, currencies, commodities) disagree.
Cut size sharply in drawdowns to flatten the equity curve; press size only when conditions are clean and trades work immediately.
After a VIX spike expect a choppy mean-reverting period; wait for a catalyst to restart trends.
Spread risk across several funding sources at 0.25-0.5% per trade instead of 1-2% in one account.
In index futures most movement is 09:30-11:00 ET and the last hour; lunch is slow - adjust from FX habits.
Searching for new systems during a drawdown does not raise the probability of the next trade.
notes: ICT-style liquidity concepts: fade sweeps of old highs/lows and of Asian/London session ranges when price closes back inside and higher-timeframe bias agrees; avoid pre-FOMC Monday/Tuesday.

style: momentum/growth breakout swing-position trader (Germany)
markets: US growth stocks; occasionally gold, oil, Bitcoin; shorts sector ETFs in bear markets
edge_principles: Limit correlated exposure: no more than three positions from the same theme/sector (a single theme-wide gap down cost 17% in one day).
Position size 10-15% of capital in good markets, 5-10% in sideways markets, up to 20-25% only in very liquid names with tight stops; ask what a 20-30% gap would do.
Equity-curve rules: cut exposure / get off margin when equity re-enters its Bollinger band after running above it, when equity drops below its 20-period MA, or after a -4% day.
Overconfidence after hot streaks leads to mediocre setups - tighten selectivity when doing well.
In bear markets stay in cash or short indices/sector ETFs rather than individual stocks (buyout squeeze risk).
Avoid 'lonely survivors': trade a stock only when its sister stocks in the theme also set up.
After a shock loss, exit quickly, review, and reset the equity-curve view to stop it dominating decisions.
notes: Bottom-up weekly screening (RS rating > 90), market trend model gate, tight consolidation/flag breakouts near the 8/21 EMA after a big initial momentum move.

style: CEO of an online equity prop/evaluation firm (Trade The Pool); ex-prop trader
markets: US stocks/ETFs (evaluation accounts)
edge_principles: Hard daily loss limits ('daily pause') act like a seatbelt and stop tilt/revenge trading.
Traders who survive funded phases start slower than in evaluation, build a profit cushion, then increase size.
Scale into positions (start with a small fraction of planned risk) to improve flexibility and confidence.
Trade the evaluation the same way you will trade funded; switching to aggressive mode after passing causes most blow-ups.
A consistency rule (no single trade > 50% of target) forces a repeatable process rather than one lucky trade.
notes: Industry/business episode: firm stats (~20-25% pass evaluation after 3-5 attempts; ~15% keep the first funded account). No trading setups.

style: news/event-driven pre-market scalper (Bulgaria, trading floor)
markets: US stocks in pre-market (small caps, Chinese ADRs, SPACs, M&A targets)
edge_principles: Analyse your own P&L by session: he made money pre-market and lost it intraday, so he restricted ~95% of trades to pre-market.
If a setup consistently loses, test trading its reverse.
Size to available liquidity; in thin pre-market books take what is offered rather than forcing size.
High win rate (~83%) scalping with immediate loss cutting avoids drawdowns (no losing month in ~18-20 months; 72 winning days in a row).
Prefer passive orders (buy the bid / sell the ask) where possible.
Learn which news types are real catalysts vs promotional PRs from serial diluters; tag them over months.
notes: Pre-market checklist per mover (news, volume, short interest, sector) then either mean-revert toward prior close or trade with the trend; specialities include fading promo news in serial-diluting micro caps and M&A fair-value pricing.

style: author (Market Wizards) and FundSeeder co-founders; trader evaluation
markets: general (all asset classes)
edge_principles: Decide the exit before the entry, while still objective (Bruce Kovner's rule).
Position size so that one bad trade cannot be catastrophic: a position can be 10% of capital but should risk only 1-2%.
Top traders treat trading as an obsession and keep a 'trainee' mindset because edges decay (index-add front-running, a time-of-day VIX pattern that stopped working after Feb 2022).
Trend following still has a rationale (policy and supply cycles persist) but whipsaws have grown; expect larger countertrend moves.
Fundamental analysis conflicts with risk management (adverse moves look like better value) and is poorly suited to timing; it is most useful contrarily when price fails to react to news.
Evaluate traders on return-to-risk (gain-to-pain, drawdown), longevity (10+ years), and strategy capacity, not raw return.
notes: Mostly about what makes Market Wizards and the FundSeeder accelerator; mentions decayed edges (index inclusion, VIX timing) but no current concrete setup.

style: intraday large-cap reversal day trader (Oliver Velez method)
markets: US large-cap stocks (TSLA, AMD, MU, MSFT, META, MSTR), SPY
edge_principles: A 30-40% win rate with 3:1-4:1 reward/risk is realistic and profitable; chasing 70-90% win rates via scalping teaches traders to cut winners and hold losers.
Keep sizing constant: he cannot predict which setup will be the big winner.
Trade only obvious levels (daily, else hourly); if you need to convince yourself it is a level, it is not.
Avoid trading inside a 'trap zone' (consolidation, e.g. prior day's last 45 minutes range).
Reversal setups fail in strong trend days; prefer ranging markets.
Allow at most two attempts at the same level.
Trade only the first hour (skip the first ~20 minutes) when participation is highest.
notes: Concrete, rules-based intraday reversal at prior-day high/low after an overextended run, plus 'elephant bar' gift-zone re-entry and a 20/200 MA state filter on 5-min charts.

style: breakout/trend trader ('Box strategy'); day trades NQ/ES, swing trades leading stocks
markets: NQ, ES futures; leading growth stocks (TSLA, COIN); manages some investor money
edge_principles: Tight lower-timeframe entries let you hold a full-size swing position while risking only ~1% of equity.
Pre-plan 2-3 scenarios each morning, max 2-3 trades/day, daily capital cap; one re-entry allowed after a stop because false breaks are common.
Scale out: half at ~1.2-1.5R, a quarter at ~3R, last part with stop at breakeven - turns many would-be losses into scratches.
Allocate to the index that is leading (ES vs NQ divergence).
Build a library of how your setup behaves in uptrends, downtrends and ranges so you can recognise regime shifts.
Avoid holding day trades through FOMC; for swings, let price confirm the trend change instead of anticipating.
Hedging against an uptrend is an emotional comfort that ties up risk capital.
notes: Box/wedge breakout after contraction, buying hourly pullbacks within a fresh daily breakout, and a two-lower-lows plus failed-breakdown bottoming pattern; uses 9 MA / 20 EMA trend gauges and observed ~12-15 pt ES rotation zones.

style: relative-strength day/short-swing trader (stocks and options), posts trades live
markets: US large-cap stocks and options; SPY
edge_principles: Cut 'indefensible' trades: OTM lottery options, counter-trend trades (shorting stocks green on the day, buying stocks red on the day); he estimates this removes ~70% of losses.
Wait for confirmation (close above the MA, conservative: open above next day) instead of front-running.
'Walkaway analysis': record price 5 min, 1 h, EOD and 2 days after each exit; most traders find holding winners ~1.5 h longer adds 30-40%.
Close decaying options instead of letting them go to zero; track the cost of not closing.
Judge performance monthly against a target band, not trade by trade.
Be optimistic when a trade is working and pessimistic when it is not (the reverse of instinct); consider adding to winners.
Trading must beat simply holding SPY or it is not worth the effort.
notes: Relative strength/weakness vs SPY day-trading method with daily-chart filters and a SPY 50-day SMA regime line; also high-probability bull put spreads below two support levels.

style: quant/HFT (ex-Citadel), Turkish equity market maker, DeFi/perp exchange builder
markets: CME futures, VIX futures/ETPs, Turkish equities, crypto DEXs and perps
edge_principles: Small operators survive by finding niches the large players overlook (complex signals rather than pure speed, emerging markets just gone electronic).
When a market is temporarily inefficient (e.g. mechanical ETP rebalancing), size up while it lasts - such alphas decay.
Hedges split across separate clearinghouses/venues are not hedges in a crash: one leg can be liquidated or auto-deleveraged while the other still stands.
Market makers can step back in extreme volatility, so order books can empty exactly when needed.
LP yields can hide adverse selection (you accumulate the falling asset).
Prefer venues with transparent, documented liquidation rules.
notes: Market-structure episode; one equity-adjacent setup: anticipating mechanical end-of-day VIX ETP rebalancing flows (now largely decayed). Crypto arbitrage/flash loans and perp mechanics described but not MCF-relevant.

style: options trader, multi-strategy fund manager (launched 2025)
markets: US stock options, SPY/QQQ and SPX 0DTE, gold index options
edge_principles: Full-porting each trade turned $3k into $80k and back to $500 in ~1.5 weeks; averaging down calls is how accounts die.
Grade every setup 1-10 and scale risk from ~1% (mediocre) to max ~5% (best); quality setups carry higher win rates.
Use limit orders; wide spreads and inflated IV on hyped small caps start trades deep underwater.
Strategy results swing with regime (trend-following longs did best in 2023); do not attribute luck to skill.
Constant tinkering with working strategies tends to lower their stats.
Note: return claims (e.g. 580% in 2024, 950% average butterfly wins) were self-reported; the show added caveats.
notes: Four strategies: daily Bollinger/RSI-divergence contrarian puts, squeeze breakout calls in uptrends, 0DTE pre-market-level break-and-retest, SPX 0DTE butterflies at gamma pin levels (high-claim, low verifiability).

guest: Compilation (Dante, Breitstein, Kellogg, Brandt, Bruzzese, Kullamagi, Shapiro, Petersson, Frolich, Moulton, Harris)
style: compilation of past-episode excerpts
markets: various
edge_principles: Bet size should be skewed: size up far more (non-linearly) on the rare exceptional setups so they outweigh the many mediocre ones (Breitstein).
Scale size with account growth and only use margin when performance has earned it (Kullamagi).
Cut losses fast; failure to do so is the most common route to ruin (Petersson).
Run trading as a business with fixed hours, preparation and end-of-period review; results lag the work by months (Frolich).
Look at P&L infrequently (monthly) to trade the market rather than the money (Moulton).
Expect 3-7 years of 'market tuition' before committing to one process (Brandt); avoid burnout from non-stop grind (Kellogg).
notes: Excerpt compilation from earlier episodes; no new setups.

style: behavioral neuroscience educator / entrepreneur (NeuroGym)
markets: none (performance psychology)
edge_principles: Distinguish 'interested' from 'committed': commitment means upgrading identity, beliefs, skills and habits to match the goal.
New behaviours need ~66-180 days of reinforcement before they override old automatic patterns; plan for a 100-day habit block.
When fear/stress spikes, first calm the nervous system (breathwork) before analysing; decisions in a stress state are myopic.
Ask what a loss would actually mean (identity, livelihood) to find the real fear behind hesitation.
Enthusiasm without skill is dangerous; separate speculation from investing.
notes: Explicitly not a trading-tactics episode; habits, identity and fear regulation. No setups. (Skimmed: content is general psychology.)

style: systematic intraday stock trader, ex-CTO Trade-Ideas, backtesting educator
markets: US stocks intraday (long and short; most profits from shorts)
edge_principles: His first backtest of his own discretionary system beat his live discretionary results - discretion in filtering was worse than he believed.
Edge often lies in which signals to skip: two traders running the 'same' system diverge because of skip rules (e.g. one skipped trades with relative volume > 3).
Backtests: judge by number of trades, not years; each added rule must tell a coherent story; keep a spare tested rule 'in the back pocket' for when the strategy degrades.
A strategy should work without stops/targets first; stops then make it worse but are required. Tight stops on 1-min bars create same-bar ambiguity that flatters backtests.
Taking half off and moving stop to breakeven tested much worse than holding full size to the natural exit.
Keep the backtest 'pristine' (commissions in, slippage/locates handled after) and reconcile live vs backtest daily, listing missed trades and why.
Scale wide (more uncorrelated strategies/trades) not just up; going from ~300 to ~3000 trades/yr via automation raised profit ~5x.
Pre-plan drawdown responses; traders quit in drawdowns, never at highs. Cutting size during a drawdown cost him in one year; not cutting cost him in the next - diversification was the fix.
notes: Core strategy: gapping stocks that form a narrowing range after the open; enter on range breakout, stop at the other side of the range, hold to the close. Tight range = large size for fixed dollar risk.
